process: "just an instance of an executing program, including the current values of the program counter (PC), registers, and variables". See [A process is a program in execution](#/comp4736-p3/process-model).
process ID|PID: The number that identifies a process; shown in brackets after the process name in pstree, e.g. main(1477) (slide 3); `getpid()` returns it. See [A process is a program in execution](#/comp4736-p3/process-model).
program counter|PC: Part of a process's state; "One program counter" in the multiprogramming figure vs "Four program counters" in the conceptual model. See [A process is a program in execution](#/comp4736-p3/process-model).
memory location|machine code|assembly co: The three columns of a disassembly: the hex address, the hex instruction bytes, and the mnemonic, e.g. 401102 / 55 / push rbp. See [A process is a program in execution](#/comp4736-p3/process-model).
text segment: "the program code" (slide 6); Linux: "Text: Program code", at the lowest address. See [Text, data, BSS, heap, stack and /proc](#/comp4736-p3/linux-address-space).
data segment: "the variables"; "The data segment grows upward" (slide 6); Linux: "Data: Initialized global (or static) variables". See [Text, data, BSS, heap, stack and /proc](#/comp4736-p3/linux-address-space).
stack segment|stack: "the stack grows downward" (slide 6); Linux: "Local variables, return address, and parameters". See [Text, data, BSS, heap, stack and /proc](#/comp4736-p3/linux-address-space).
gap: The unused space between the data segment and the stack in the three-segment figure. See [A process is a program in execution](#/comp4736-p3/process-model).
BSS|Block Started by Symbols: "Block Started by Symbols. Uninitialized global (or static) variables". See [Text, data, BSS, heap, stack and /proc](#/comp4736-p3/linux-address-space).
heap: The region above BSS that grows upward toward the stack (slide 47); shown as `[heap]` in /proc/PID/maps. See [Text, data, BSS, heap, stack and /proc](#/comp4736-p3/linux-address-space).
kernel space|user space: Kernel space sits at the higher addresses above the stack; user space runs from stack down to text. See [Text, data, BSS, heap, stack and /proc](#/comp4736-p3/linux-address-space).
multiprogramming: "The rapid switching back and forth is called multiprogramming"; the CPU switches from process to process quickly, runs each for tens or hundreds of milliseconds, and at any one instant runs only one process. See [A process is a program in execution](#/comp4736-p3/process-model).
process switch: The jump of the one program counter from one process to the next in the multiprogramming figure. See [A process is a program in execution](#/comp4736-p3/process-model).
conceptual model: "Conceptual model of four independent, sequential processes", each with its own program counter. See [A process is a program in execution](#/comp4736-p3/process-model).
foreground process: Processes created at boot that are "interacting with (human) users and perform work for them". See [The four events that create a process](#/comp4736-p3/process-creation).
background process: Processes that "run in the background and are not associated with particular users, but instead have some specific function". See [The four events that create a process](#/comp4736-p3/process-creation).
daemon: "Processes that stay in the background to handle some activity such as email, Web pages, news, printing, and so on are called daemons". See [The four events that create a process](#/comp4736-p3/process-creation).
system initialization: Process-creation event 1: "When an operating system is booted, typically numerous processes are created". See [The four events that create a process](#/comp4736-p3/process-creation).
process-creation system call by a runnin: Process-creation event 2: "Often a running process will issue system calls to create one or more new processes to help it do its job". See [The four events that create a process](#/comp4736-p3/process-creation).
user request to create a new process: Process-creation event 3: "users can start a program by typing a command or (double) clicking on an icon". See [The four events that create a process](#/comp4736-p3/process-creation).
initiation of a batch job: Process-creation event 4: "applies only to the batch systems found on large mainframes … When the operating system decides that it has the resources to run another job, it creates a new process and runs the next job from the input queue in it". See [The four events that create a process](#/comp4736-p3/process-creation).
normal exit: Termination condition 1 (voluntary): "Most processes terminate because they have done their work". See [The four ways a process ends, and process hierarchies](#/comp4736-p3/process-termination).
error exit: Termination condition 2 (voluntary): "the process discovers a fatal error", e.g. `cc foo.c` with no such file: "the compiler simply announces this fact and exits". See [The four ways a process ends, and process hierarchies](#/comp4736-p3/process-termination).
fatal error: Termination condition 3 (involuntary): "an error caused by the process, often due to a program bug. Examples include executing an illegal instruction, referencing nonexistent memory, or dividing by zero". See [The four ways a process ends, and process hierarchies](#/comp4736-p3/process-termination).
killed by another process: Termination condition 4 (involuntary): "the process executes a system call telling the operating system to kill some other process". See [The four ways a process ends, and process hierarchies](#/comp4736-p3/process-termination).
exit: The UNIX system call a process uses "to tell the operating system that it is finished". See [The four ways a process ends, and process hierarchies](#/comp4736-p3/process-termination).
ExitProcess: The Windows equivalent of exit. See [The four ways a process ends, and process hierarchies](#/comp4736-p3/process-termination).
kill: The UNIX call that tells the OS to kill some other process; "the killer must have the necessary authorization to do in the killee". See [The four ways a process ends, and process hierarchies](#/comp4736-p3/process-termination).
TerminateProcess: "The corresponding Win32 function" to kill. See [The four ways a process ends, and process hierarchies](#/comp4736-p3/process-termination).
signaled: "a process can tell the operating system that it wishes to handle certain errors itself, in which case the process is signaled (interrupted) instead of terminated". See [The four ways a process ends, and process hierarchies](#/comp4736-p3/process-termination).
parent process|child process: "when a process creates another process, the parent process and child process continue to be associated in certain ways. The child process can itself create more processes". See [The four ways a process ends, and process hierarchies](#/comp4736-p3/process-termination).
process group: "In UNIX, a process and all of its children and further descendants together form a process group"; a keyboard signal "is delivered to all members of the process group currently associated with the keyboard". See [The four ways a process ends, and process hierarchies](#/comp4736-p3/process-termination).
handle: In Windows, "a special token … that it [the parent] can use to control the child"; the parent "is free to pass this token to some other process, thus invalidating the hierarchy". See [The four ways a process ends, and process hierarchies](#/comp4736-p3/process-termination).
running: "actually using the CPU at that instant". See [Running, Ready, Blocked and the four transitions](#/comp4736-p3/process-states).
ready: "scheduled and runnable; temporarily stopped to let another process run". See [Running, Ready, Blocked and the four transitions](#/comp4736-p3/process-states).
blocked: "unable to run until some external event happens". See [Running, Ready, Blocked and the four transitions](#/comp4736-p3/process-states).
transition 1|Running → Blocked: "Process blocks for input"; "occurs when the operating system discovers that a process cannot continue right now". See [Running, Ready, Blocked and the four transitions](#/comp4736-p3/process-states).
transition 2|Running → Ready: "Scheduler picks another process"; "occurs when the scheduler decides that the running process has run long enough, and it is time to let another process have some CPU time". See [Running, Ready, Blocked and the four transitions](#/comp4736-p3/process-states).
transition 3|Ready → Running: "Scheduler picks this process"; "occurs when all the other processes have had their fair share and it is time for the first process to get the CPU to run again". See [Running, Ready, Blocked and the four transitions](#/comp4736-p3/process-states).
transition 4|Blocked → Ready: "Input becomes available"; "occurs when the external event for which a process was waiting (such as the arrival of some input) happens". See [Running, Ready, Blocked and the four transitions](#/comp4736-p3/process-states).
pause: A system call some systems provide so a process can get itself into blocked state. See [Running, Ready, Blocked and the four transitions](#/comp4736-p3/process-states).
scheduler|process scheduler: "a part of the operating system"; causes transitions 2 and 3 "without the process even knowing about them". See [Running, Ready, Blocked and the four transitions](#/comp4736-p3/process-states).
process table: "a table (an array of structures) … with one entry per process"; the entry holds the program counter, stack pointer, memory allocation, open-file status, accounting and scheduling information, and everything that must be saved when the process is switched from running to ready or blocked "so that it can be restarted later as if it had never been stopped". See [The process table, the PCB and the context switch](#/comp4736-p3/process-table).
process table entry fields: Process management (registers, program counter, program status word, stack pointer, process state, priority, scheduling parameters, process ID, parent process, process group, signals, time when process started, CPU time used, children's CPU time, time of next alarm), memory management (pointers to text, data and stack segment info), file management (root directory, working directory, file descriptors, user ID, group ID). See [The process table, the PCB and the context switch](#/comp4736-p3/process-table).
context switch: "the process of saving the current state of a running process and loading the saved state of another process so that it can resume execution". See [The process table, the PCB and the context switch](#/comp4736-p3/process-table).
PCB|Process Control Block: "a data structure that represents a single process in the operating system. The PCB is a crucial component within the process table"; the context (program counter, register values, other state) is saved into it. See [The process table, the PCB and the context switch](#/comp4736-p3/process-table).
user-level context|ucontext_t: Per the code comment, includes "1) signal mask, 2) stack info, 3) link to next context, and an embedded machine-level context (mc)"; captured by `getcontext`, restored by `setcontext`. See [The process table, the PCB and the context switch](#/comp4736-p3/process-table).
machine-level context|mc: "General-purpose registers: RIP, RSP, RAX, etc.". See [The process table, the PCB and the context switch](#/comp4736-p3/process-table).
interrupt vector: "Associated with each I/O class is a location (typically at a fixed location near the bottom of memory) called the interrupt vector"; the hardware "loads new program counter from interrupt vector". See [What the lowest level of the OS does when an interrupt occurs](#/comp4736-p3/interrupts).
interrupt handling skeleton: The eight steps the lowest level of the OS does when an interrupt occurs: hardware stacks PC; hardware loads new PC from interrupt vector; assembly saves registers; assembly sets up new stack; C interrupt service runs; scheduler decides which process runs next; C returns to assembly; assembly starts up new current process. See [What the lowest level of the OS does when an interrupt occurs](#/comp4736-p3/interrupts).
Interrupt Vector Table|IVT: "Interrupt Vector Table of x86 processors running in real mode": 4-byte IP:CS entries for INT 0x00-0xFF from address 00000000 up to 000003F0+0C. See [What the lowest level of the OS does when an interrupt occurs](#/comp4736-p3/interrupts).
I/O wait fraction|p: "a fraction p of its time waiting for I/O to complete". See [CPU utilization = 1 − pⁿ](#/comp4736-p3/modeling-multiprogramming).
degree of multiprogramming|n: The number of processes in memory at once; x-axis of the utilization curve. See [CPU utilization = 1 − pⁿ](#/comp4736-p3/modeling-multiprogramming).
CPU utilization: "CPU utilization = 1 − pⁿ"; pⁿ is "the probability that all n processes are waiting for I/O (in which case the CPU will be idle)"; the model "assumes that all n processes are independent". See [CPU utilization = 1 − pⁿ](#/comp4736-p3/modeling-multiprogramming).
CPU waste: The idle fraction pⁿ, e.g. "CPU waste = (0.8)¹⁰ ≈ 0.1074". See [CPU utilization = 1 − pⁿ](#/comp4736-p3/modeling-multiprogramming).
fork(): Creates a child process; the parent gets fork_return_value = child_pid (e.g. 4509), the child gets fork_return_value = 0. See [fork(), parent_pid 4508 and child 4509, and the stripped-down shell](#/comp4736-p3/fork-and-the-shell).
parent_pid|child_pid: The parent's own PID (e.g. 4508) and the new child's PID (e.g. 4509) in the fork figure. See [fork(), parent_pid 4508 and child 4509, and the stripped-down shell](#/comp4736-p3/fork-and-the-shell).
stripped-down shell: Loop that types a prompt, reads a command, forks; the parent does `waitpid(−1, &status, 0)` ("wait for child to exit") and the child does `execve(command, parameters, 0)` ("execute command"); "TRUE is assumed to be defined as 1". See [fork(), parent_pid 4508 and child 4509, and the stripped-down shell](#/comp4736-p3/fork-and-the-shell).
waitpid|wait(): Parent call that waits for a child to exit (slide 49); in the zombie figure, the parent's wait() that cleans up the child. See [Zombie and orphan processes](#/comp4736-p3/zombies-and-orphans).
execve|exec(): Call the child uses to execute a command. See [fork(), parent_pid 4508 and child 4509, and the stripped-down shell](#/comp4736-p3/fork-and-the-shell).
/proc|proc filesystem: "a pseudo-filesystem which provides an interface to kernel data structures. It is commonly mounted at /proc"; "Every process in Linux is represented by a directory in /proc". See [Text, data, BSS, heap, stack and /proc](#/comp4736-p3/linux-address-space).
/proc/PID/maps: A file in the process's /proc directory showing the "process address space". See [Text, data, BSS, heap, stack and /proc](#/comp4736-p3/linux-address-space).
pstree: "display a tree of processes", e.g. `pstree -p -T`. See [pstree, ps, top and the state letters D I R S T X Z](#/comp4736-p3/linux-process-states).
ps: "report a snapshot of the current processes", e.g. `ps aux`. See [pstree, ps, top and the state letters D I R S T X Z](#/comp4736-p3/linux-process-states).
top: "display Linux processes" (slide 54); columns PID = Process ID, USER = User name, PR = Priority, NI = Nice value, VIRT = Virtual Image, RES = Resident size, SHR = Shared Mem size, S = Process Status, %CPU = CPU usage, %MEM = Memory usage. See [pstree, ps, top and the state letters D I R S T X Z](#/comp4736-p3/linux-process-states).
htop: The interactive variant of top shown in the tools slides. See [pstree, ps, top and the state letters D I R S T X Z](#/comp4736-p3/linux-process-states).
D|uninterruptible sleep: "uninterruptible sleep (usually IO and cannot be killed)" (slide 59); leaves to R on "wake up". See [pstree, ps, top and the state letters D I R S T X Z](#/comp4736-p3/linux-process-states).
I|idle kernel thread: "Idle kernel thread". See [pstree, ps, top and the state letters D I R S T X Z](#/comp4736-p3/linux-process-states).
R|running or runnable: "running or runnable (on run queue)". See [pstree, ps, top and the state letters D I R S T X Z](#/comp4736-p3/linux-process-states).
S|interruptible sleep: "interruptible sleep (waiting for an event to complete and can be killed)" (slide 59); leaves to R on "wake up/signal". See [pstree, ps, top and the state letters D I R S T X Z](#/comp4736-p3/linux-process-states).
T|stopped: "stopped by job control signal" (slide 59); entered from R on SIGSTOP, back to R on SIGCONT. See [pstree, ps, top and the state letters D I R S T X Z](#/comp4736-p3/linux-process-states).
X|dead: "dead (should never be seen)". See [pstree, ps, top and the state letters D I R S T X Z](#/comp4736-p3/linux-process-states).
Z|zombie|defunct: "defunct ("zombie") process, terminated but not reaped by its parent" (slide 59); entered from R on Exit(). See [pstree, ps, top and the state letters D I R S T X Z](#/comp4736-p3/linux-process-states).
<|high-priority: "high-priority (not nice to other users)". See [pstree, ps, top and the state letters D I R S T X Z](#/comp4736-p3/linux-process-states).
N|low-priority: "low-priority (nice to other users)". See [pstree, ps, top and the state letters D I R S T X Z](#/comp4736-p3/linux-process-states).
+|foreground process group: "is in the foreground process group". See [pstree, ps, top and the state letters D I R S T X Z](#/comp4736-p3/linux-process-states).
SIGSTOP|SIGCONT: The signals labelled on the Linux state diagram: SIGSTOP takes R to T, SIGCONT takes T back to R. See [pstree, ps, top and the state letters D I R S T X Z](#/comp4736-p3/linux-process-states).
zombie process: Created "when the parent process does not wait for the child process termination. A zombie process doesn't consume many system resources, but it does continue to live in the system's task list"; "The parent process is responsible for waiting for child process to terminate and then cleaning up the child process entry from the process table". See [Zombie and orphan processes](#/comp4736-p3/zombies-and-orphans).
orphan process: "The parent dies (or terminates) before its child … The child process will be automatically adopted by the init process". See [Zombie and orphan processes](#/comp4736-p3/zombies-and-orphans).
init: "the parent of all the processes with the pid of 1" (slide 67); PID 1 is /sbin/init in the Ubuntu ps and htop screenshots (slides 13, 58) and tini(1) in the container screenshots. See [pstree, ps, top and the state letters D I R S T X Z](#/comp4736-p3/linux-process-states).
